content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors study weighted (adaptive) regularization for single layer neural networks. They apply adaptive regularization for L1 as well as nuclear norm separately, arrive at formal statements for model and structure recovery. In the experiments, they show that the weighted regularization achieves better performance and recovery than the non-weighted counterparts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strength of the paper are the formal statements for model and structure recovery, which appear new (to the reviewer's knowledge). 

Weakness
- The adaptive Lasso and its variants are quite popular and the extension of them towards the single layer NNs doesn't appear much novel. 
There seem to be few relevant works which the submission missed out. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.10825.pdf
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00180-021-01190-4

- Theorem 6.2 provides the bound when the solution W_{N, 1} and W_{N, *} are within a fixed radius of the optimal solution. Given that neural networks have difficulty in initialization, how practically useful is this reuslt ?

- Similarly, do the results of Theorem 6.3 also apply when the solutions W_{N, 1} and W_{N, *} are within a fixed radius of the optimal solution?

- The experiments are also weak. The simulated experiments may benefit from various settings of d, K, initializations, etc. 

- The numerical results on the real datasets are inconclusive. As given in Table 1, non-weighted one gives better results for some of the datasets, while weighted L1 does better in some others. Also, the additional level of sparsity typically leads to inferior accuracy in the models, Hence whether this adaptive approach works for the accuracy of interest is not fully understood. However the weighted regularization works better for the nuclear norm as evidenced from Table 2.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to follow. The paper is limited by its novelty and the comprehensiveness of the study which ultimately affects the quality.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while the formal statements may be interesting, this work may need significant improvements in terms of the experimental comparisons and establishing relations to other relavent work on adaptive regularizatin on neural networks.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a sparsity-inducing regularization technique for deep learning models. The main motivation for the method is the adaptive selection of regularization coefficients for all the weights individually. Namely, the authors propose the following algorithm. First, they train the model without any regularization just by minimizing the objective $f_N(\cdot)$, i.e.

$\widehat{W}_N = \underset{W}{\operatorname{argmin}} f_N(W).$

Second, they train the model once again, but now putting L1 regularization on every weight with the coefficients inversely proportional to $\widehat{W}_N$. Additionally, they penalize for L2 distance to $\widehat{W}_N$. The final optimization problem is then

$\min_{W} f_N(W) + \lambda_N  ||W-\widehat{W_N}||^2 + \gamma_N \sum_{i,j} \frac{|W(i,j))|}{|\widehat{W}_N(i,j)|}.$

The authors also propose another version of the algorithm where they put the nuclear matrix norm instead of L1.

The authors provide both theoretical and empirical analysis of the proposed algorithm. The theoretical result is summarized in two theorems. Theorem 6.1 states the convergence of unregularized optimization to the set of global optimizers. Theorem 6.2 states qualitatively the same result but for the proposed algorithm. As I understand from Section 4, the authors assume throughout the paper that the set of global optimizers contains sparse solutions.

For the empirical study of the proposed algorithm, the authors demonstrate its performance on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny-ImageNet using ResNet and VGG architectures. For different sparsity levels, they report classification accuracy and compare the proposed algorithm against sparse models obtained via L1-regularization.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The idea of the algorithm extends the idea of Adaptive Group Lasso proposed and analyzed in [5] (with further studies in [4]). Theoretical results are mostly an adaption of the results from [4] (theorems 3.4, 3.6) to the proposed scenario. Thus, the novelty of the paper and its main contribution boils down to the adaptation of the technique from [4,5] to individual weights and bringing it to the deep learning domain.

My major concerns are regarding the empirical study of the proposed algorithm. First of all, the baseline choice is questionable. Indeed, the comparison to vanilla L1 regularization is reasonable; however, the community developed many more efficient sparsification techniques over years, including very relevant ones that adaptively regularize parameters. For instance, I can enumerate adaptive regularization that converges to low-rank solutions [1], adaptive sparsity techniques [2], and layer-adaptive sparsification via optimization [3].

The second major concern is performance gain. In most cases, the performance gain is either marginal or lies within a large standard deviation interval, which is evaluated by $3$ independent runs. Given that the baseline is the most basic sparsification method, the practical value of the proposed algorithm is questionable.

1. Zhao H, Tsai YH, Salakhutdinov RR, Gordon GJ. Learning neural networks with adaptive regularization. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2019;32.
2. Lee J, Park S, Mo S, Ahn S, Shin J. Layer-adaptive sparsity for the magnitude-based pruning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.07611. 2020 Oct 15.
3. Chen T, Ji B, Shi Y, Ding T, Fang B, Yi S, Tu X. Neural network compression via sparse optimization. arXiv preprint arXiv:2011.04868. 2020 Nov 10.
4. Dinh VC, Ho LS. Consistent feature selection for analytic deep neural networks. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2020;33:2420-31.
5. Dinh V, Ho LS. Consistent feature selection for neural networks via Adaptive Group Lasso. arXiv preprint arXiv:2006.00334. 2020 May 30.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, the paper is well structured, and the main results are clearly exposed. However, the paper has a lot of minor presentation issues. The non-extensive list of examples is given below.

1. The following sentence on page 3 uses subjective descriptions to motivate the approach. However, these terms are mostly confusing and do not provide any intuition to the reader.
"the same regularization coefficient for each element in the parameter matrix without distinguishing the importance of the elements, which is unfair and will make the estimation value of the really important elements small"
2. Typo on page 4. "For \forall"
3. On page 4, the third paragraph, the first sentence has a punctuation error.
4. On page 4, the third paragraph, the second sentence lacks a subject.
5. Remark 5.1 uses notation, which is not introduced: $C_{\delta_1}, \nu, L_1, L_2, L_3$.
6. In the appendix, sections with theorems proofs are titled "proof of lemma...".
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a sparsification algorithm, which is inspired mostly by previous works introducing Adaptive Group Lasso. The authors adapt theoretical results from previous works and demonstrate the applicability of the proposed technique for deep learning methods on image recognition benchmarks. The empirical study demonstrates marginal improvement compared to sparsification via L1 regularization.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
